candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find the first question worth asking' and the speech and language therapist viewpoint suggested the question a swallowing specialist asks before anything else: how do the tablets actually go down. The other words (library card, weather forecasting) gave nothing.
candidates.working_title: Before a tablet is crushed
candidates.core_insight: Difficulty swallowing tablets is common and often unspoken, and crushing, splitting or opening some products (modified-release, enteric-coated and others) changes how they work, so ask how tablets are being taken and check with a pharmacist before altering any of them.
candidates.angle: Medicine reviews ask what is taken and rarely ask how it is swallowed. The workaround that carers and staff reach for out of kindness, crushing into food, is unsafe for some products, and a pharmacist can usually offer a liquid, dispersible or patch alternative.
candidates.position: Anyone reviewing an older person's medicines should ask how the tablets are swallowed, and no tablet should be crushed, split or opened until a pharmacist has confirmed it is safe to do so.
claims_needing_evidence: A substantial minority of older adults report difficulty swallowing tablets or capsules (community survey studies, e.g. Schiele 2013).

Crushing modified-release tablets can release the whole dose at once, and crushing enteric-coated tablets removes their protection (pharmacy guidance: Specialist Pharmacy Service, NEWT, BNF general guidance, product SPCs).

In an observational study in UK care homes with nursing, administration errors occurred in 57.3% of observed administrations for residents with dysphagia and 30.8% for residents without (Serrano Santos 2016).
Pharmacists can often suggest an alternative formulation or route for people with swallowing difficulty (Specialist Pharmacy Service guidance).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'apply it to the poorest or most isolated person' and the ward clerk viewpoint turned attention to the discharge paperwork and what it assumes about who is at home to collect, chase and check new medicines.
candidates.working_title: The medicines handover that assumes someone at home
candidates.core_insight: People leaving hospital on new medicines, especially those who live alone, should ask how many days of each new medicine they are taking home, who will arrange the next supply and by when, and whether their community pharmacy has been told what changed.
candidates.angle: Apply the discharge medicines plan to the person with nobody to phone the GP: the gap between the hospital supply running out and the first repeat prescription is where people without an advocate fall.
candidates.position: Hospitals should not rely on unpaid relatives to complete the medicines handover; for people who live alone, the handover to GP and community pharmacy should be arranged before they leave (ethical and service judgement, marked as such).
claims_needing_evidence: Medication-related harm after discharge is common in older people in England: 413 of 1,116 people aged 65 or over followed for 8 weeks (Parekh 2019, PRIME cohort).

Hospitals supply a limited quantity of new medicines at discharge and ongoing supply then comes from the GP (NHS trust discharge policies; RPS transfer of care guidance). Supply length varies and must not be stated as a single figure.
In England, the NHS Discharge Medicines Service lets hospitals refer patients to their community pharmacy with details of medicine changes (NHS England service specification, from February 2021).
An English evaluation found electronic referral from hospital to community pharmacy was associated with lower readmission (Nazar 2016); observational, so association only.
Arrangements differ in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland (check each before stating anything nation-specific).

candidates.opening_line_draft: The supply of new medicines you take home from hospital runs out, and someone has to arrange the next one before it does.
candidates.visual_idea: Question card with three questions: How many days of each new medicine am I taking home? Who arranges the next supply, and by when? Has my community pharmacy been told what changed? Drawn illustration of an older man at his own front door with a hospital bag and a pharmacy bag.
candidates.pause: People who live alone, and relatives who live far away, recognise the scramble when discharge tablets run out.
candidates.gain: Three specific questions that close a common gap after discharge.
candidates.follow: Signals that the account pays attention to people without an advocate.
candidates.earlier_overlap: E142 (medication review after delirium as a named task) and E145 (hospital-started sleeping tablet) concern what is on the list at discharge; this concerns supply and handover for people living alone. Different point.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'find an outcome patients value that the routine measure misses', with the home care worker viewpoint and the words queuing and defaults, pointed to the daily timetable of doses and the care visits built around it.
candidates.working_title: Count the times of day, not only the tablets
candidates.core_insight: The number of separate times each day a person has to take medicines is part of treatment burden in its own right, and a review can often reduce it even when no medicine is stopped.
candidates.angle: Routine reviews count medicines; people and home carers live with the timetable. Four dosing times can mean four interruptions or four care visits a day. A trial of regimen simplification reduced dosing times, and it also reported more falls in the simplified group, driven mainly by one site, which the post must state.
candidates.position: Medicines reviews for older people should record and try to reduce the number of daily dosing times as well as the number of medicines, and watch for unintended effects when timings change.
claims_needing_evidence: In the SIMPLER cluster randomised trial in Australian residential aged care, structured regimen simplification reduced the mean number of daily medication administration times by 0.47 at 12 months (95% CI 0.09 to 0.84) compared with the comparison arm (Sluggett 2020).
Simplification was possible for 62 of 99 residents in the intervention arm (Sluggett 2020).

SIMPLER observed a higher incidence of falls in the intervention arm over 12 months (IRR 2.20), mainly driven by one facility; hospitalisation and mortality did not show clear differences (Sluggett 2020). This must be reported.
Regimen complexity, including number of administration times, can be measured (Medication Regimen Complexity Index; George 2004).
People describe the work of taking medicines as part of treatment burden (Tran 2015 taxonomy; Duncan 2018 MTBQ).
For people receiving home care, medicines support is tied to visit times (NICE NG67, 2017).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'compare the stated aim of a service with what happens' and the viewpoint of a researcher designing a trial led to the chain from finding inappropriate prescriptions to changing outcomes; the words counting and sequence shaped a stepwise diagram.
candidates.working_title: Fewer inappropriate medicines, same admissions
candidates.core_insight: In the OPERAM trial, a structured medicines review reduced inappropriate prescribing in older inpatients but did not show fewer drug-related readmissions, so changing a medicines list and changing outcomes are separate steps that each need measuring.
candidates.angle: Read a medication review trial as a chain: problems found, recommendations made, recommendations carried out, changes kept, outcome changed. Effects can be lost at each step, and the outcome chosen may not be the one patients value most.
candidates.position: Medication review is worth doing, and claims that it reduces admissions should be tested rather than assumed; trials and services should report each step of the chain and outcomes that patients value.
claims_needing_evidence: OPERAM enrolled 2,008 adults aged 70 or over with multimorbidity and polypharmacy in four European countries (Blum 2021).
86.1% of intervention participants had inappropriate prescribing, with a mean of 2.75 STOPP/START recommendations each (Blum 2021).
62.2% of intervention participants had at least one recommendation implemented at 2 months (Blum 2021).
First drug-related hospital admission within 12 months occurred in 21.9% of the intervention group and 22.4% of the control group (hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.17) (Blum 2021).

In a UK cohort, prescription of Beers-listed medicines at discharge was not significantly associated with overall medication-related harm (Parekh 2019), consistent with list-based measures being imperfect proxies for harm.
The SENATOR trial also did not show a clear reduction in adverse drug reactions (O'Mahony 2020) (check before use).

candidates.stimulus_use: The quality 'reversibility' and the process 'returning', with the night nurse viewpoint (someone who watches for what comes back), suggested presenting a stop as a planned, reversible trial with named things to watch.
candidates.working_title: A trial off, planned like a trial on
candidates.core_insight: Stopping a long-term medicine can usually be treated as a planned trial: agree what to watch for, who will watch, when to look again and what would mean restarting.
candidates.angle: People fear stopping because it feels permanent and can feel like being given up on. For most medicines a stop can be reversed, and the commonest problem after stopping is the original condition returning, which a plan can catch early.
candidates.position: Every decision to stop a long-term medicine should come with a plan for what to watch, when to review and when to restart.
claims_needing_evidence: In a study of older outpatients, most medicines that were stopped were not followed by an adverse withdrawal event, and 88% of the events that did occur were the underlying condition returning (Graves 1997).
Deprescribing guidance recommends a planned process with tapering where needed, monitoring and review (Scott 2015; Scottish Government Polypharmacy Guidance).
Some medicines need to be reduced gradually rather than stopped suddenly (BNF; deprescribing guidelines).

candidates.gain: A structure that makes stopping safer and less frightening.
candidates.follow: Decision support that treats starting and stopping as equally deliberate.

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the scale' moved from the single consultation, where a prescriber may assume this patient wants to keep every tablet, to a population survey of what older people say they want.
candidates.working_title: Most older people say they would stop a medicine if their doctor said they could
candidates.core_insight: In a US population survey, 92 in 100 older adults said they would be willing to stop one or more regular medicines if their doctor said it was possible, so prescribers should offer the option rather than assume reluctance.
candidates.angle: Patient reluctance is often cited as the barrier to deprescribing. Scaled up to a population, older people's stated attitudes point the other way, and those on six or more medicines were more willing. Stated willingness in a survey is still different from agreement in a consultation.
candidates.position: Prescribers should raise the option of stopping medicines instead of assuming older people want to keep them all.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 1,981 US Medicare beneficiaries aged 65 or over, 92.0% (weighted) said they would be willing to stop one or more regular medicines if their physician said it was possible (Reeve 2018).
66.6% (weighted) wanted to reduce the number of medicines they take (Reeve 2018).
People taking 6 or more medicines had higher odds of being willing (adjusted odds ratio 2.90); do not convert to 'times more likely' (Reeve 2018).
Prescribers report patient resistance as a barrier to deprescribing (primary source needed, e.g. Anderson 2014 systematic review; the statement in Reeve 2018 is background only).
UK data on patient attitudes to deprescribing, if any, should be checked for consistency.

candidates.working_title: Write why it was stopped
candidates.core_insight: When a medicine is stopped or changed in hospital, the discharge letter should say why and what would justify review, because without the reason the next prescriber may simply restart it.
candidates.angle: A medicines change without a reason is incomplete information: the GP, the pharmacist and the patient each have to guess, and a repeat prescription can undo a deliberate decision.
candidates.position: Every medicine stopped, started or changed at discharge should carry a one-line reason and, where relevant, a line on what should prompt review.

The PRSB eDischarge summary standard includes medication changes with a reason (check current version).
Studies of discharge communication find that reasons for medicine changes are often missing (e.g. Kripalani 2007 review; Grimes 2011) (check figures before use).
Medicines stopped in hospital are sometimes restarted after discharge (primary care study needed; drop this claim if no source is found).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'look at the smallest practical detail' with the quality 'residue' and the night nurse viewpoint led to the used pain patch: the drug left in it, the old patch left on, and heat from a hot water bottle or electric blanket at night.
candidates.working_title: A used patch still contains medicine
candidates.core_insight: Strong pain patches such as fentanyl or buprenorphine need three habits: take the old patch off before putting a new one on, keep heat sources off the patch, and fold used patches sticky sides together before safe disposal.
candidates.angle: Patches look like the low-effort option compared with tablets, which makes their specific hazards easy to miss: a forgotten old patch adds to the dose, heat speeds absorption, and a discarded patch can still harm a child or a pet.
candidates.position: Anyone caring for a person who uses an opioid patch should be shown these three checks by the prescriber or pharmacist.
claims_needing_evidence: Used fentanyl patches still contain a substantial amount of active drug after the wearing period (product SPC; MHRA Drug Safety Update on accidental exposure).
External heat increases absorption of fentanyl from patches and has been linked with overdose (fentanyl SPC; MHRA; FDA safety communications).
Buprenorphine patches carry similar warnings about heat (buprenorphine patch SPC).
Applying a new patch without removing the old one is a recognised error (MHRA or NHS patient safety reports) (check source).
Used patches should be folded with the adhesive sides together and disposed of as the pharmacist advises (SPC and patient leaflet).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'name the trade-off openly' with the words order of events and rewinding led to the trade-off inside deprescribing: stopping several things quickly versus one at a time so that any change can be traced back.
candidates.working_title: Stopping has side effects too
candidates.core_insight: Stopping a medicine has its own adverse effects, mostly the original condition returning and sometimes withdrawal reactions, so deprescribing should be tapered where needed, done one change at a time where possible, and followed up.
candidates.angle: Deprescribing is often presented as risk-free subtraction. Data on adverse drug withdrawal events show it is an intervention with its own side-effect profile, and in one study the number of medicines stopped was the only factor linked with events.
candidates.position: Treat deprescribing as an intervention: taper drugs with known withdrawal effects, change one thing at a time where possible, arrange review, and tell the person that the slower pace is a deliberate trade-off.
claims_needing_evidence: Of 238 medicines stopped in 124 older outpatients, 62 (26%) were followed by an adverse drug withdrawal event (Graves 1997).
88% of these events were exacerbations of the underlying disease, and 36% led to hospitalisation or an emergency or urgent care visit (Graves 1997).
Only the number of medicines stopped was associated with the occurrence of an event (Graves 1997).
In D-PRESCRIBE, 38% of people who attempted to taper sedative-hypnotics reported withdrawal symptoms and no adverse events requiring hospitalisation were reported (Martin 2018).

Drug classes with recognised withdrawal or rebound effects include benzodiazepines, beta-blockers, antidepressants, corticosteroids, proton pump inhibitors, antiepileptics and levodopa (BNF; deprescribing safety reviews).
Limitations to state: Graves 1997 is an old, small, retrospective study from one US Veterans Affairs clinic; newer data should be sought.

candidates.working_title: Medicines for a future the person may not have
candidates.core_insight: Many older people near the end of life are still taking preventive medicines whose benefits take years to appear, and reviewing them with the person or family when goals shift towards comfort is part of good care.
candidates.angle: The number of different medicines rises through the last year of life, partly from long-term preventive drugs that were never reviewed. When swallowing is hard, each unnecessary tablet costs comfort.
candidates.position: When a person's goals shift towards comfort, preventive medicines with a long time to benefit should be reviewed with them or their family; stopping them changes the treatment plan and does not withdraw care.
claims_needing_evidence: Among 511,843 people over 65 who died in Sweden in 2007 to 2013, the proportion exposed to 10 or more different drugs rose from 30.3% to 47.2% over the final year of life (Morin 2017).
15.8% were using a statin in their final month of life (Morin 2017).
Among 5,406 US nursing home residents with advanced dementia, 53.9% received at least one medication judged to be of questionable benefit (Tjia 2014).

In a pragmatic trial in people with an estimated life expectancy of 1 month to 1 year, stopping statins did not meet the prespecified noninferiority criterion for death within 60 days (23.8% versus 20.3%), and total quality of life was slightly better in the group that stopped (Kutner 2015). Report this accurately and do not call stopping 'proven safe'.
Preventive medicines such as statins have a time to benefit measured in years (time-to-benefit literature, e.g. Holmes 2013).
Guidance on care in the last days of life includes reviewing medicines (NICE NG31, 2015) (check wording).

candidates.stimulus_use: The operation 'change the viewpoint to someone else in the scene' and the quality 'small print' moved the viewpoint from the prescriber to the person reading the leaflet from the box at home.
candidates.working_title: What 'common' means in a medicine leaflet
candidates.core_insight: In UK medicine leaflets, 'common' means up to 1 in 10 people, 'uncommon' up to 1 in 100 and 'rare' up to 1 in 1,000, and people given the words alone tend to overestimate the risk by a large margin.
candidates.angle: The leaflet words have fixed numerical meanings that most readers do not know. In a UK study, people told a side effect was 'common' estimated a risk of about a third on average, when the figure was 2.5%.
candidates.position: Leaflets and clinicians should give numbers alongside the frequency words; readers should know what each word means.
claims_needing_evidence: The EU and UK labelling convention defines very common (1 in 10 or more), common (1 in 100 to 1 in 10), uncommon (1 in 1,000 to 1 in 100), rare (1 in 10,000 to 1 in 1,000) and very rare (fewer than 1 in 10,000) (European Commission SmPC guideline, 2009; patient leaflet wording 'may affect up to 1 in 10 people').
In a randomised study of 120 UK adults taking statins, those told constipation was 'common' estimated its likelihood at 34.2% on average, compared with 8.1% for those told '2.5%' (Knapp 2004).
For pancreatitis described as 'rare', mean estimates were 18% with the word and 2.1% with the number 0.04% (Knapp 2004).
Verbal descriptors were associated with more negative views of the medicine (Knapp 2004).

candidates.working_title: Same medicine, different-looking tablet
candidates.core_insight: Generic tablets can change colour or shape when the pharmacy's supplier changes; if tablets look different, check the name and strength on the box, or ask the pharmacist, before stopping them or taking extra.
candidates.angle: People and carers who recognise medicines by appearance can be caught out by a change nobody mentioned. In a large US study, changes in pill colour or shape were linked with people stopping important heart medicines.
candidates.position: Pharmacies should tell people when a tablet's appearance changes, and people should check the label rather than the look of a tablet.
claims_needing_evidence: In a US claims study of people after a heart attack, 29% had a change in the colour or shape of a generic cardiovascular medicine during the year (Kesselheim 2014).
The odds of stopping the medicine were higher after a colour change (adjusted odds ratio 1.34) and after a shape change (adjusted odds ratio 1.66); observational, association only (Kesselheim 2014).
A similar association has been reported for antiepileptic drugs (Kesselheim 2013) (check).
In the UK, generic prescribing means the manufacturer supplied can differ between dispensings (NHS or Royal Pharmaceutical Society source needed).

candidates.working_title: Doctors could not tell who would be harmed by their medicines after discharge
candidates.core_insight: In an English cohort, more than a third of older people had medication-related harm within 8 weeks of discharge, and discharging doctors' predictions of who would be harmed did not match who was, so medicines follow-up after discharge should not depend on clinical hunch.
candidates.angle: The finding that should change practice is the prediction result, alongside the incidence: if judgement at discharge does not pick out who is at risk, follow-up targeted by hunch will miss people.
candidates.position: Older people leaving hospital on changed medicines should have routine medicines follow-up, for example through community pharmacy, rather than follow-up only for those a clinician judges to be at risk.
claims_needing_evidence: In the PRIME cohort (English teaching hospitals, 2013 to 2015), 413 of 1,116 people aged 65 or over followed for 8 weeks after discharge (37%) had medication-related harm (Parekh 2019).
Medication-related harm in PRIME included adverse drug reactions, non-adherence and medication errors (Parekh 2019).
Discharging doctors' predictions of medication-related harm requiring healthcare showed no clear link with actual harm (odds ratio 1.10, 95% CI 0.82 to 1.46), whatever their experience (Parekh 2018).
85% of predictions were made by doctors with less than 5 years' experience (Parekh 2018).
Frailty was associated with healthcare use due to medication-related harm, independent of number of medicines (Stevenson 2022).

candidates.stimulus_use: Following the event over time produced a second idea: what happens after a successful stop, when a trial ends and support is withdrawn.
candidates.working_title: Stopping psychotropics reduced falls; keeping them stopped was the hard part
candidates.core_insight: In a small blinded trial, gradual withdrawal of psychotropic medicines in older people reduced falls, and the authors reported that permanent withdrawal was very difficult to achieve, so deprescribing for falls needs follow-up over months.
candidates.angle: Deprescribing trials are reported at their end point. The harder question is what happens months later, when support stops and sleep or anxiety problems return.
candidates.position: Plans to withdraw sedating or psychotropic medicines to prevent falls should include support and review over months, not a single stop.
claims_needing_evidence: In a 2 by 2 factorial randomised trial of 93 people aged 65 or over taking psychotropic medicines in Dunedin, gradual blinded withdrawal gave a relative hazard for falls of 0.34 (95% CI 0.16 to 0.74) over 44 weeks (Campbell 1999).
The authors concluded that permanent withdrawal is very difficult to achieve (Campbell 1999 abstract); the number who restarted after the trial must be taken from the full text.
The World Falls Guidelines recommend medication review with deprescribing of fall-risk-increasing drugs (Montero-Odasso 2022).
STOPPFall lists fall-risk-increasing drug classes with deprescribing considerations (Seppala 2021).
The relative hazard must not be converted to an absolute risk without the event counts.

candidates.core_insight: When giving a medicines list, include eye drops, inhalers, patches, creams, injections given at a clinic or every few months, medicines supplied by a hospital clinic, and anything bought from a shop or pharmacy, because these are easily left off.

candidates.working_title: The leaflet counts side effects, not benefits
candidates.core_insight: Medicine leaflets list side effects with frequencies but usually give no figure for how likely the medicine is to help or how long that takes, so people deciding whether to keep taking a medicine see only half the picture; ask the prescriber or pharmacist for the benefit in numbers.
candidates.angle: The standard leaflet has a detailed, graded side-effects section and a short, unquantified 'what it is used for' section. The imbalance can push people to stop medicines that would have helped them, and trials of balanced 'facts boxes' show a better alternative.
candidates.position: Information given with medicines should state likely benefit as clearly as likely harm; until it does, people should ask for it.

Reviews of written medicines information found leaflets give little information on benefits (Raynor 2007) (check).

candidates.working_title: Swollen ankles after amlodipine: the prescribing cascade
candidates.core_insight: Ankle swelling after starting a calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine is a recognised side effect, and treating it with a loop diuretic adds a second drug with its own harms; the first step is to reconsider the first drug.
candidates.angle: Prescribing cascades are easy to describe and hard to see from inside a record. Population data from Ontario show the calcium channel blocker to loop diuretic cascade happens at scale, and it persists for up to a year.
candidates.position: Before treating a new symptom in an older person, check whether a recently started medicine explains it; for calcium channel blocker oedema, reduce or switch the drug rather than add a diuretic.
claims_needing_evidence: Among adults aged 66 or over with hypertension in Ontario, those newly dispensed a calcium channel blocker had a higher cumulative incidence of loop diuretic dispensing at 90 days than those newly dispensed another antihypertensive or an unrelated drug (1.4% versus 0.7% and 0.5%) (Savage 2020).
The association persisted, slightly attenuated, up to 1 year and in the amlodipine-only subgroup (Savage 2020).
Calcium channel blocker oedema arises from arteriolar dilation and responds poorly to diuretics (pharmacology review, e.g. Sica 2003).
The prescribing cascade was described by Rochon and Gurwitz (BMJ 1997).
ThinkCascades lists clinically important cascades in older people (McCarthy 2022).

candidates.working_title: The kidney number to dose from
candidates.core_insight: For some medicines, including direct oral anticoagulants, doses should be calculated from creatinine clearance using the Cockcroft-Gault equation, because eGFR can overestimate kidney function in small, older people with low muscle mass and lead to overdosing.
candidates.angle: The eGFR on the lab report is convenient and adjusted to a standard body size; many dosing recommendations use Cockcroft-Gault, and the two diverge most in the people geriatric services see: very old, light, low-muscle patients.
candidates.position: For direct oral anticoagulants and other renally cleared drugs with narrow margins, calculate creatinine clearance with actual body weight in older people, especially those who are frail or at extremes of weight.
claims_needing_evidence: MHRA advised in 2019 that creatinine clearance calculated with the Cockcroft-Gault formula should be used to dose direct oral anticoagulants and certain other drugs, and in older people and those at extremes of muscle mass or weight (MHRA Drug Safety Update, 2019; check month and wording).
eGFR is normalised to 1.73 m2 body surface area and may overestimate kidney function in people with low muscle mass (NICE NG203; MHRA).
Serum creatinine depends on muscle mass, so a creatinine in the normal range can accompany reduced kidney function in a person with low muscle mass (NICE NG203; renal physiology source).
Studies in older people with atrial fibrillation show eGFR and Cockcroft-Gault place many patients in different anticoagulant dose categories (comparison study needed) (unsure).

candidates.working_title: Parkinson's medicines on the person's own times
candidates.core_insight: People with Parkinson's often take their medicines at precise, individual times; in hospital, ask for doses at the person's own times, ask whether they can keep taking their own, ask for a plan if they are unable to swallow or are nil by mouth, and ask that anti-sickness drugs that block dopamine are avoided.
candidates.angle: Hospital drug rounds run at ward times, while Parkinson's medicine timing is individual. Missed or late doses and dopamine-blocking drugs are linked with longer stays, and families can prevent some of this with a written list on day one.
candidates.position: Parkinson's medicines are time-critical and should be given at the person's own times in hospital (judgement supported by guidance); families are right to ask for this.
claims_needing_evidence: In 1,628 people with Parkinson's admitted to 11 public hospitals in the Basque Country in 2011 to 2012, medication errors (omitted or mistimed dopaminergic doses, or centrally acting antidopaminergic drugs) affected almost a third of admissions and were associated with a median 4-day longer stay and higher in-hospital mortality; observational (Lertxundi 2017).
Some anti-sickness medicines, such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine, and most antipsychotics block dopamine and can worsen Parkinson's (NICE NG71; BNF).
Levodopa should not be withdrawn abruptly (NICE NG71).
Non-oral options, such as a rotigotine patch, can be considered when oral medicines are not possible (NICE NG71; Parkinson's UK guidance).
Parkinson's UK runs the Get It On Time campaign, and an HSIB investigation examined time-critical Parkinson's medication (check both).

candidates.working_title: Which tablets to pause when you are ill, and when to restart
candidates.core_insight: People taking metformin, ACE inhibitors or ARBs, water tablets, SGLT2 inhibitors or anti-inflammatory painkillers should ask their GP or pharmacist in advance which to pause during an illness that stops them keeping fluids down, and when to restart.
candidates.angle: Sick day rules are sensible and widely used; the evidence behind them is limited and the restart instruction is easily forgotten. The useful move is a personal plan agreed while well, rather than a generic card.

Dehydration increases the risk of acute kidney injury with these medicines; metformin is linked with lactic acidosis in acute kidney injury, and SGLT2 inhibitors with ketoacidosis (BNF; MHRA).

candidates.working_title: A booklet that helped people stop long-term sleeping tablets
candidates.core_insight: In a Canadian trial, sending long-term benzodiazepine users aged 65 or over a booklet on the risks with a tapering plan led 27 in 100 to stop within 6 months, compared with 5 in 100 without it; a later pharmacist-led version had similar results.

62% of intervention recipients started a conversation about stopping with a physician or pharmacist (Tannenbaum 2014).
Age over 80, duration of use and polypharmacy did not significantly modify the effect (Tannenbaum 2014).

candidates.working_title: Ask whether it is being taken before deciding it has failed
candidates.core_insight: Between a third and a half of medicines prescribed for long-term conditions are not taken as recommended, often for reasons the person can explain, so ask about medicine-taking without blame before increasing a dose or adding a drug.
candidates.angle: Apparent treatment failure is sometimes a medicine that is not being taken. Escalating the dose on paper produces a list that no longer matches what happens at home, and the reason for not taking it (a side effect, a belief, a practical problem) is useful clinical information.

NICE recommends asking about adherence in a way that does not apportion blame (NICE CG76; check wording).

candidates.working_title: Daily aspirin 'just in case' after 70
candidates.core_insight: For people aged 70 or over who have never had a heart attack or stroke, a large trial found daily low-dose aspirin did not help them live longer free of disability and increased serious bleeding; people who take aspirin because of a past heart attack, stroke or stent should not stop without advice.

The largest trial in healthy older people found no benefit on the outcome most would value and more serious bleeding, and the distinction between prevention in healthy people and treatment after a heart attack or stroke is what readers most need.
candidates.position: If you are over 70, take daily aspirin and have never had a heart attack, stroke or other artery disease, ask your GP or pharmacist whether you still need it; do not stop aspirin prescribed after a heart attack, stroke or stent without advice.

All-cause mortality was higher in the aspirin group (5.9% versus 5.2%), mainly from cancer, and the authors advised caution in interpretation (McNeil 2018, mortality paper).

candidates.working_title: When a good HbA1c is a warning
candidates.core_insight: For frail older people with diabetes, an HbA1c that looks well controlled while they take insulin or a sulfonylurea can come with frequent low blood sugars, and guidelines support relaxing targets and reducing these medicines.
candidates.angle: A low number can be a sign of overtreatment. US national data found tight control was as common in people in poor health as in healthy people, often achieved with insulin or sulfonylureas, the drugs most likely to cause low blood sugar.

UK guidance for older people with frailty recommends individualised targets and avoiding hypoglycaemia (Strain 2018 or other UK source; check).
Hypoglycaemia in older people is linked with falls and hospital admission (observational evidence needed).

candidates.working_title: A blister pack is an answer to one kind of problem
candidates.core_insight: Multi-compartment compliance aids (blister packs, dosette boxes) help some people with some adherence problems, are unsuitable for some medicines, make tablets harder to identify and doses harder to change, and should follow an assessment of what the problem actually is.

candidates.working_title: Heartburn after stopping an acid tablet can be a rebound
candidates.core_insight: After stopping a proton pump inhibitor (an acid-reducing tablet such as omeprazole or lansoprazole), heartburn can return for a few weeks as a temporary rebound, even in people who never had heartburn, so a gradual step-down with a plan is more likely to succeed than stopping and restarting at the first symptom.
candidates.angle: Rebound symptoms are usually taken as evidence that the tablet is still needed. A trial in healthy volunteers found the tablet itself produced acid symptoms after it was stopped.
candidates.position: People stopping long-term proton pump inhibitors should be warned about rebound and offered a step-down plan; some people do need them long term.
claims_needing_evidence: In a randomised trial of 120 healthy volunteers, 44% (26 of 59) of those given esomeprazole 40 mg for 8 weeks followed by placebo reported at least one clinically relevant acid-related symptom in weeks 9 to 12, compared with 15% (9 of 59) given placebo throughout (Reimer 2009).
A deprescribing guideline recommends reducing the dose or changing to use when needed for adults who have completed treatment for mild to moderate reflux, and advises about rebound (Farrell 2017).
Some people need long-term proton pump inhibitors, for example with Barrett's oesophagus, severe oesophagitis or a history of bleeding ulcers (Farrell 2017; NICE CG184).
Limitation to state: the trial was in healthy volunteers after 8 weeks of treatment; older long-term users may differ.
